text: A wise son heeds his father's discipline, but a mocker will not listen to rebuke.
From the fruit of his mouth a man eats what is good, but the appetite of the treacherous is for violence.
Whoever guards his mouth protects his life, but the one who opens his lips wide comes to ruin.
The sluggard craves and gets nothing, but the desires of the diligent are richly satisfied.
The righteous hates falsehood, but the wicked brings on himself stench and shame.
Righteousness guards the one whose way is blameless, but wickedness overthrows the sinner.
One pretends to be rich, yet has nothing; another pretends to be poor, yet has great wealth.
A rich man's wealth may ransom his life, but the poor man hears no threat.
The light of the righteous shines brightly, but the lamp of the wicked is snuffed out.
Where there is arrogance, there is strife, but wisdom is with those who take advice.
Wealth gained by fraud dwindles away, but whoever gathers little by little makes it grow.
Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life.
Whoever despises the word will suffer for it, but the one who fears the commandment is rewarded.
The teaching of the wise is a fountain of life, turning a person from the snares of death.
Good sense wins favor, but the way of the treacherous is hard.
Every prudent person acts with knowledge, but a fool parades his folly.

versions.text: The prudent act with knowledge in all they do, but a fool parades his folly.
versions.explanation: In Hebrew כָּל modifies עָרוּם ("every prudent one"), not the action; the current rendering shifts the scope to "in all they do." It also mixes plural ("the prudent act") with singular in the second line ("a fool parades"), which is jarring when read aloud.

text: A wicked messenger falls into trouble, but a faithful envoy brings healing.

versions.text: A wicked messenger brings disaster, but a faithful envoy brings healing.
versions.explanation: The verb יִפֹּל בְּרָע means "falls into evil/trouble" — the messenger himself suffers harm. "Brings disaster" reverses the direction of the action and loses the contrast with the reward implied for the trustworthy envoy.

text: Poverty and disgrace come to the one who ignores discipline, but whoever heeds correction is honored.
A desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul, but turning from evil is detestable to fools.

versions.text: A desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul, but fools refuse to turn from evil.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew says turning from evil is an "abomination" (תּוֹעֵבָה) to fools. "Refuse" weakens the strong term and loses the parallel structure of "sweet" versus "detestable."

text: Walk with the wise and become wise; keep company with fools and come to harm.
Disaster pursues sinners, but the righteous are rewarded with good.
A good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children, but the sinner's wealth is stored up for the righteous.
The fallow ground of the poor yields abundant food, but injustice sweeps it away.
Whoever spares the rod hates his son, but the one who loves him is diligent to discipline him.
The righteous eats his fill, but the belly of the wicked goes hungry.
